question: What are the two-pointer and sliding window patterns in Python and when do you apply them?
title: Two Pointers and Sliding Window
direct_answer: Two pointers uses two indices that move toward each other (or in the same direction) to reduce O(n²) nested loops to O(n). Sliding window maintains a window of elements, expanding and shrinking as needed — used for subarray/substring problems with a constraint. Both work on sorted arrays or strings. Common uses: two sum in sorted array, longest substring without repeats, maximum sum subarray of size k.
interviewer_intent: Tests pattern recognition — whether the candidate can reduce brute-force O(n²) solutions to O(n) with a standard technique.

sections.title: Two-pointer and sliding window patterns
sections.content:
These are reduction patterns — they transform O(n²) brute force into O(n) by maintaining state across iterations instead of restarting from scratch.

Two-pointer (converging): start left=0, right=len-1. Move them toward each other based on a condition. Classic use: find two numbers in a sorted array that sum to target. If sum > target, move right left. If sum < target, move left right.

Two-pointer (same direction): both pointers move forward but at different speeds (fast/slow for cycle detection) or one skips elements (remove duplicates from sorted array in-place).

Sliding window: maintain a window [left, right] over the array. Expand by moving right, shrink by moving left. Keep a constraint (window size, no duplicate chars, etc.). The window 'slides' forward. Classic use: longest substring without repeating characters — right expands until a repeat is found, then left advances past the duplicate.

The mental model for choosing: if you need to find a pair or triplet in a sorted array → two pointers. If you need to find a subarray or substring satisfying a constraint → sliding window.

sections.title: Pattern implementations
Pattern selection guide
items: Two pointers (converging): sorted array, find pair with property
Two pointers (same direction): in-place array modification, fast/slow for cycles
Sliding window: subarray/substring with constraint, O(n) instead of O(n²)
Sliding window fixed size: track sum, slide by adding right - removing left[i-k]
Sliding window variable size: left pointer shrinks window when constraint violated

speakable_v2.hook: Two pointers and sliding window are the O(n) refactors for problems that look like they need O(n²) nested loops.

beats.content: Two pointers: left starts at 0, right at the end, they move toward each other. At each step you decide which pointer to move based on whether the current state satisfies, overshoots, or undershoots the target. Sorted array is required for this to work.

Sliding window: right expands the window, left shrinks it. You maintain a constraint — no duplicate chars, sum under limit, etc. When the constraint is violated, advance left until it holds again. The window slides forward, touching each element at most twice.

items: Sorted array, find pair → two pointers converging
Subarray sum or substring property → sliding window
Linked list cycle → fast/slow two pointers

speakable_v2.cap: If you're writing a nested loop over an array and the inner loop starts at i+1, ask yourself: can I reduce this to O(n) with two pointers?
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Good follow-up: three-sum extending two pointers, or minimum window substring as a harder sliding window.
